article_title: Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings
citation: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: NFTE's entrepreneurial mindset framework of eight core domains
description: NFTE conceptualizes the entrepreneurial mindset as a 21st century skill set comprising eight core domains: Future Orientation, Comfort with Risk, Opportunity Recognition, Initiative and Self-Reliance, Communication and Collaboration, Creativity and Innovation, Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, and Flexibility and Adaptability. The report states that "an individual who acts and thinks like an entrepreneur has an entrepreneurial mindset." NFTE grounds the framework in the claim that non-cognitive skills are malleable and can improve with instruction, and its programs pair entrepreneurial-mindset skill growth with small-business-management content instruction.
requirements: Programs must provide students the support and experiences needed to develop the mindset, via project-based lessons and experiential activities
constraints: The framework is NFTE's own articulation (NFTE, 2016b); the report treats it as a program-defined construct rather than an independently validated taxonomy
target_learners: middle and high school students in under-resourced communities
target_learning_goals: entrepreneurial mindset skills such as opportunity recognition, communication and collaboration, and critical thinking
examples: NFTE programs teach the domains through business plan creation, business plan competitions, experiential activities such as the Buying and Selling Event and the Product Innovation Game, and Community Walks
key_sources: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED582976

article_title: Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings
citation: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: NFTE Startup Summer intensive business startup program
description: Startup Summer is NFTE's most intensive startup program, targeting a select group of students ready to launch the business they planned in Owning Your Future or Startup Tech. It begins with a Boot Camp week in which students set goals, create marketing materials, and plan initial launch steps; participants then meet three times per week for six weeks, receive an investment grant and stipend, meet volunteer business coaches, and can pitch in a Shark Tank-style event. Since 2011 approximately 150 students have participated.
requirements: Students complete an application toward the end of their classroom program and are selected as ready to launch with mentoring and eventual funding
constraints: The program is selective and small (approximately 150 participants since 2011), offered initially in New York City and later Los Angeles and South Florida
target_learners: high school students from under-resourced communities ready to launch a planned business
target_learning_goals: business launch skills, marketing, goal setting, and entrepreneurial mindset application
examples: The 2016 alumni survey found 71 percent of Startup Summer respondents launched a business and 83 percent frequently used what they learned at NFTE at their current work
key_sources: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED582976

article_title: Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals
citation: Zhou, W., Nan, W., Xiong, K., & Ku, Y. (2024). Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals. npj Science of Learning 9, 32. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00242-w
title: Neurofeedback training protocols should use engaging feedback interfaces and enough sessions to support long-term learning
description: Based on their finding of within-session but not across-session alpha learning, the authors argue that feedback design and training dose matter. "Motivational factor is one predictor of NF success, and the learning eﬃciency of NF training will be improved by the participant ’s t r o n g motivation." They note most studies up-regulate alpha via visual feedback (e.g., a face changing to smiling or crying) and that successful long-term NF learning could be obtained by more than five training sessions.
requirements: An engaging feedback interface to sustain participant motivation
More than five training sessions to obtain successful long-term NF learning
constraints: In this study a blue-bar feedback interface and five sessions yielded short-term but not across-session alpha enhancement; the article also notes a fixed 8–12 Hz band did not account for inter-individual alpha-frequency differences
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of EEG alpha activity for cognitive enhancement
examples: Participants kept a blue bar high via real-time alpha amplitude at Pz; after the experiment some participants reported feeling bored during NF training, and five daily sessions were delivered
key_sources: Zhou, W., Nan, W., Xiong, K., & Ku, Y. (2024). Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals. npj Science of Learning 9, 32. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00242-w

article_title: Need for Cognition Predicts Academic Interest Development but Not the Other Way Around: A Longitudinal Study of Secondary School Students.
citation: Matthes Julia, Scherrer Vsevolod, Preckel Franzis. (2025). Need for Cognition Predicts Academic Interest Development but Not the Other Way Around: A Longitudinal Study of Secondary School Students. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14262
title: NFC as a person-related facilitator of academic interest development
description: The article positions need for cognition—a stable tendency to "engage in and enjoy effortful cognitive activity"—as a person-related variable that helps trigger and maintain academic interest development, consistent with the Four-Phase Model of Interest Development and PPIK theory. The authors interpret their longitudinal finding as showing that "NFC seems to contribute to a learning context that is particularly beneficial for the development of academic interest possibly by interacting with the content of interest via positive affect, information search, knowledge acquisition, effort, and persistence." Unlike domain-specific interest, NFC is domain-general.
requirements: Requires longitudinal or process-oriented designs to identify in which phase of interest development NFC operates, which the authors state their data cannot address
constraints: The authors state their data do not allow statements about individual phases of interest development or specific functional relations over time
Findings come from German high-track (Gymnasium) students and cannot be generalized to lower-track schools or other countries without further investigation
target_learning_goals: development of academic interest in mathematics, German, and English
examples: The study tested this account with autoregressive cross-lagged panel models over four waves, finding NFC predicted later interest but not vice versa
key_sources: Matthes Julia, Scherrer Vsevolod, Preckel Franzis. (2025). Need for Cognition Predicts Academic Interest Development but Not the Other Way Around: A Longitudinal Study of Secondary School Students. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14262

article_title: Need for Cognition Predicts Academic Interest Development but Not the Other Way Around: A Longitudinal Study of Secondary School Students.
citation: Matthes Julia, Scherrer Vsevolod, Preckel Franzis. (2025). Need for Cognition Predicts Academic Interest Development but Not the Other Way Around: A Longitudinal Study of Secondary School Students. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14262
title: NFC-Teens scale (11 positively worded items)
description: The NFC-Teens scale is a self-report measure of need for cognition for adolescents, adapted from Cacioppo and Petty's adult NFC scale into German. In this study only the 11 positively worded items (of 19) were used to avoid item-wording effects, with answers on a five-point Likert scale; a sample item is "I like to do tasks that require me to think a lot." Internal consistency ranged from McDonald's ω = 0.89 to ω = 0.92 across the four measurement points, and the shortened scale correlated r = 0.91 with the total scale.
requirements: Administered as part of a student questionnaire; construct validity supported in prior studies including a latent correlation of r = 0.99 with another NFC scale
constraints: The article notes prior findings of positive and negative item-wording effects, which motivated using only positively worded items
target_learning_goals: measuring students' tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful cognitive activity
examples: Used at three of the four measurement occasions in the PULSS longitudinal study
key_sources: Matthes Julia, Scherrer Vsevolod, Preckel Franzis. (2025). Need for Cognition Predicts Academic Interest Development but Not the Other Way Around: A Longitudinal Study of Secondary School Students. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14262
